Above the 10% floor — rebuilt this week

reports.note: The cash floor was restored to 17.6%, and that is the only credit on offer. The oversized names sat untouched — SRPT near 31%, SPCX at −29%, SERV through its stop — and new positions went on with no written thesis behind them. The engine is sound. The discipline around it is not.

The market did most of the −4% — marks on names already held; realized activity was quiet. But the controllable leak, SRPT at 30% of the book, stayed wide open two weeks after it was flagged. Cash discipline was the only line held.

reports.note: A +1.2% bounce handed over by the tape, and it was spent: the reserve went to 1.7% and a losing directional (SPCX −23%) got averaged up. Greener week, thinner margin for error. The controllable leaks widened while the marks recovered.

dials.rule: Top name under the 20% cap · SRPT (was 30%) fully offloaded

reports.note: The turn. SRPT — 30% of the book for three weeks — was fully offloaded via assignment, taking cash from 1.7% to 30.8% and sizing back under the cap. First clean sweep on all three dials. Standing watch: SERV is through its −15% stop, and SPCX bounced on luck rather than thesis. Neither becomes the next SRPT.

dials.rule: Top name under the 20% cap · three names above 15%
Back above the 10% floor after the NU assignment · sat at 0.7% mid-week
No event contract since Aug 6 · JPUSD flat since Aug 5

reports.note: All three dials closed clean. They did not stay clean. The 30.8% reserve taken off the SRPT exit was committed across three sessions into NU, NIQ, XNDU, PLTR, SPCX and BBAI, running cash to 0.7% and gross to 1.09× by midweek. Friday's expiry reversed it: the NU $15 calls were assigned, 300 shares called away at the strike, reserve rebuilt to 16.7%, book back under 1×. Credit where it is due — that exit was pre-arranged by the covered call, the strategy working as designed. But the floor was breached for two days first, and that was a decision, not an accident. +3.2% on the week, the cap held, the sleeve stayed shut.

buckets.name: Covered-call premium
buckets.note: The engine. Premium taken on shares already held — managed, rolled, and bought back cheap. This is the line that pays.

buckets.name: Share legs
buckets.note: Where the casualties are. A small number of oversized names, not a failure of selection.

buckets.name: Event contracts
buckets.note: High-volume churn at break-even, negative once costs are counted. Decommissioned — activity mistaken for work.

insights: Loss asymmetry is the leak. The average loser runs 1.7× the average winner, so a 60% hit rate still finishes behind. The targets are being picked correctly; the losses are being let off the leash.
The engine is real: covered-call premium takes 78% of its closes at a 3.7 profit factor. That is the business. Everything else is management around it.
The event sleeve is shut, not shrinking — nothing traded since Aug 6. It was 91% of all closes for effectively no contribution, and retiring it strips the loudest noise out of the record.
Share legs run a 0.23 profit factor across 33 closes, nearly all of it traceable to two names held past their stops. The per-name cap is scar tissue from this line.
The honest read: profit factor slipped from 0.92 to 0.88 this month and payoff from 0.61 to 0.59. Marks recovered faster than the realized record did, and marks are not money.

constraints.title: Mandate — what this account may trade
permitted: Selling covered calls against held shares
constraints.note: Interactive Brokers restricts this account to selling covered calls. Cash-secured puts — a core strategy in the principal's personal account and the preferred way to get long a name — are not permitted here, and no position is structured to work around the restriction. A mandate expansion is under review pending a business-plan revision.

p: The book is a concentrated set of retail-momentum equities held as collateral and worked for premium with covered calls. SRPT was cut in early August, freeing roughly a third of the account; that capital was committed across the book inside a week, and Friday's NU assignment handed a working reserve back. Cash sits near 17%, gross exposure under 1× — no leverage in use, and no single name over the 20% cap. The event-contract sleeve is shut: nothing open, nothing planned.

ul: Covered-call premium on liquid small-cap momentum names — the engine, and the only line that reliably pays.
Cash is materiel, not an idle balance — held to be committed, most recently resupplied by assignment.
Directional holds taken sparingly, sized small, each carrying a written thesis and a stop set before entry.
The event-contract sleeve is decommissioned. The book is equities and covered calls.
Hard cap of 20% of NAV in any single name — held this week at 18.6%.
No leverage — gross exposure about 0.92× NAV, cash near 17% against a 10% floor.
Broker mandate restricts options activity to selling covered calls (see Operations).
Sizing, reserve, and event exposure inspected every week — findings published whether or not they flatter.

concepts.h: What we hold to be true
ul: Harvest premium. Do not chase direction.
Size is the risk lever. The entry is not.
Define the loss before taking the position.
Most of the tape is noise. Separating it is the work.

p: A handful of durable ideas carry the book: asymmetry — small, defined risk against convex payoff; premium taken from names the crowd overpays to insure; and the discipline to accept that sizing, not selection, is where most books are killed.
Looking like a mad hatter today and being right over the long run is the intended outcome, provided the fundamentals underwrite the view.

The watchlist runs across financials, defense, technology, and petrochemicals. Themes under current interest: artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications, credit and insurance, and founder-led firms — with several more held off the page.

discipline.h: The largest position is the trader
p: The principal risk to this book is not the tape — it is the person marking it. Conviction that turns into size. A winner that talks you into a bigger bet. A loser held because selling it makes the loss real. Temperament is the position that has cost the most, and the control framework exists to constrain it rather than to trust it.

ul: Concentration — no more than 20% of NAV in any single name. A hard limit, not a target.
Liquidity — a 10% cash floor at all times. Dry powder is a position, and it is the one that buys the dislocation.
Loss control — stops marked before the order goes in, and honored. No averaging down a broken thesis.
Thesis — every position carries one before it is sized. The typical trade runs entry, target, exit; investments are held outright and not collateralized.

p: Positions are marked daily; the limits are tested every Friday in the after-action. Three dials — concentration, cash floor, event exposure — each passed or breached, and the week is graded on discipline rather than on P&L alone. A green week with a breached limit still grades badly. Breaches are not quietly closed out: cash ran to 0.7% against a 10% floor in the week to Aug 14, and that sits in the permanent record next to the +3.2%.

One oversized position gave back months of grinding. The per-name limit, the cash floor, and the stop discipline are scar tissue — written down so the lesson does not get paid for twice. Limits are set when the book is calm and enforced when it is not. That is the whole reason they are written down at all.

This is a single-manager book. There is no independent risk function here and no second line of defence, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. It compensates the only way it can: the limits are mechanical, the tests are identical every week, and the results are published whether or not they flatter. Self-reporting is worth nothing unless the failures appear too.

Pareidolia is the mind's tendency to see meaningful patterns — faces — in random noise. The idea started as a university capstone and was rebuilt for markets: read the world like an operator, keep the fundamentals in hand, and accept looking like a mad hatter today if the long arc proves the read.
No house view and no consensus to hide behind. We form the read ourselves, size it deliberately, and let a written framework — not the mood of the tape — hold the book.

Pareidolia was built from the ground up, on partner capital and no outside scaffolding. The intent was never to stay small — it is to compound a durable, inspectable process into something far larger, one disciplined decision at a time.
